turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.heard: pick the project that best shows mobile skills
card.say: Good evening, and thank you for the introduction. The project I'd pick is the product page at KKday, because it's the most hands-on Android work I've done. Travelers used it to choose a tour, a date and a ticket type, and the price and stock had to update on every tap. Before my change, each tap took about one second, which felt slow. I rebuilt how the data was prepared, moved the heavy calculation off the main thread, and sent results through StateFlow.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a real project (KKday product page), its users (travelers choosing tour/date/ticket), the problem (slow ~1s per tap), and the candidate's own scope (rebuilt data prep, moved calculation off main thread, used StateFlow), with no invented employers, titles, or numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the KKday product page, you said you rebuilt how the data was prepared and moved the heavy calculation off the main thread — which exact parts of that did you build yourself versus the rest of the team?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: which parts did you build yourself
card.say: I built the SKU calculation myself. I flattened the configuration and built the price and stock index. I moved the work to Dispatchers.Default and sent results through StateFlow. The caching and skeleton screens were also my work. The backend product data and the design came from other teams.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies which parts the candidate personally built (SKU calculation, price/stock index, Dispatchers.Default, StateFlow, caching, skeleton screens) versus what came from other teams, which is consistent with the earlier answer and adds specificity without inventing any employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: walk one user action through the path
card.say: I'll take one tap on a ticket type. The tap goes to the ViewModel, and it updates the selected options in a StateFlow. The calculation runs on Dispatchers.Default, not on the main thread. It looks up the price and stock in the index I built ahead of time, then sends the new result back through StateFlow. The screen collects that state and redraws the price and stock.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a ticket-type tap through ViewModel, StateFlow, Dispatchers.Default, the prebuilt price/stock index, and back to the screen collecting state — covering UI, state, and data layers — and identifies the changed logic (off-main-thread calculation and index lookup). It contains no invented numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, first suspicion, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a wrong price after a fast double tap. My first guess was the network, so I logged the request and response. The data was correct every time. Then I reproduced it by tapping two options quickly. The second tap read the old index before the first result came back.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline — first suspicion (network), evidence that overturned it (logged request/response showed correct data, then a fast double-tap repro), and root cause (second tap read the old index before the first result returned), with observations (data correct every time) distinguished from conclusions (the stale-index root cause).
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said the second tap read the old index before the first result came back — how did you actually confirm that was the root cause rather than just a plausible story?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: how did you confirm the root cause, not just a plausible story
card.say: I confirmed it with a log line. I printed the selected option and the index version each time the calculation ran. In the fast double tap, the second line showed the old version number. When I added the version check, the wrong price stopped. I also ran the same double tap ten times before and after the fix.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer adds specific new evidence (a log line printing selected option and index version, the old version number appearing on the second tap, the version check fixing it, and ten repeated double-tap runs before/after), which directly confirms the root cause rather than restating the earlier story. It stays consistent with the prior answers (index built ahead of time, StateFlow, Dispatchers.Default, double-tap bug) and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: other options, why not them, how did you know it worked after release
card.say: I had two other options. One was to lock the calculation with a mutex, so only one ran at a time. The other was to cancel the old job when a new tap came in. I didn't pick the mutex because it would still queue the taps and make the page feel slow. I didn't pick cancel-and-restart because a fast double tap would throw away the first result, and the user would see a flicker.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two real alternatives (mutex, cancel-and-restart) and the constraint ruling each out (queued taps feel slow; flicker from discarded result), and it cites a test as the source of the result (ten double-tap runs before and after the fix) — though it does not state that test's limits, the criterion's examples are covered at least twice and nothing stated is wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: delivery risk, team disagreed, who decided, what I finished
card.say: At KKday, I found a broken back button in some old pages during testing, just before a release. I told the project manager that same day. I gave two options: ship everything else and move my change to the next release, or ship it all and accept the risk. He decided to move my change. I kept checking the other pages and fixed the back button myself.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete case (broken back button before release), states when and whom (told the project manager that same day), two options offered, that the PM decided, and what the candidate personally did (kept checking pages and fixed the back button), all attributed to KKday.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: You said the PM chose to move your change and you fixed the back button yourself — before that release, what risk were you personally willing to accept, who watched the data afterward, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Tell the story of the KKday product page project: users, problem, and where my responsibility started and ended
card.heard: what risk I accepted, who watched the data, what signal would pause or roll back
card.say: I was willing to accept the risk on the pages I hadn't checked yet, because the back button only affected navigation, not prices or orders. I told the PM that clearly, so he decided with the real picture. For the release, I ran the checks we already had: the fast double tap ten times, the price and stock on each option, and the back button on every page I could reach. Everything else shipped on time. After release, I watched the crash rate in Bugly and the reports from QA and support.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer adds specifics (risk scope limited to unchecked pages, Bugly crash-rate monitoring, QA/support reports, the concrete check list) rather than repeating the prior answer, and stays consistent with the earlier KKday story (back button fix, double-tap testing, PM decision). It invents no new employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.heard: design a mobile wallet, clarify requirements, define the MVP path
card.say: Before I design anything, I'd like to check a few things. Who are the users: friends sending money to each other, or a business paying people? Where does the money balance really live: only on our server, or also with a bank or card partner? And what should work offline: can someone start a transfer with no network, or should the app just show the last known balance? Does that match what you want?
card.then: Wait for the interviewer to confirm the scope.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer asks about stored balance vs external rail (server vs bank/card partner), offline behaviour, and user scope, and it proposes an MVP path (friends sending money to each other).
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: rules given, draw client, server and local storage
card.say: Okay, the rules are clear. The screen shows the balance and the transfer form, and it only reads state from the ViewModel. The ViewModel calls the repository, and the repository is the only place that talks to the network and the local database.
card.type: draw@wallet architecture: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Screen: balance, transfer form] --> B[ViewModel: state] ⏎   B --> C[Repository] ⏎   C --> D[Local DB: cached balance and history] ⏎   C --> E[Server API] ⏎   E --> F[Ledger: accounts, transfers]
card.then: Next I'd walk through one transfer from A to B, step by step.

more: The board already shows the three parts. The screen and ViewModel own only what the user sees. The repository owns the data rules, and the local database is a cache for offline reads. The server owns the ledger, so it decides every balance and limit.

diagram.type: draw@wallet architecture: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Screen: balance, transfer form] -->

judge.detail: PASS: The mermaid flowchart correctly shows the client layers (Screen → ViewModel → Repository → Local DB) plus the Server API and Ledger, and the SAY correctly assigns ownership to each part, explicitly stating the server owns the ledger and decides every balance and limit (the authority).
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the Android client (UI, ViewModel, repository, local database), the server and its ledger; SAY says what each part owns and that the server ledger is the authority.

turns.name: W2-seq
turns.question: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars. A confirms on the screen, and the ViewModel sends the transfer to the repository. The repository writes a pending record to the local database and sends the request with a client transfer ID. The server checks A's balance, then debits A and credits B in one transaction. A goes from 100 to 20 dollars, and B goes from 0 to 80.
card.type: draw@wallet sequence: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as Screen and ViewModel ⏎   participant R as Repository ⏎   participant D as Local DB ⏎   participant S as Server ⏎   participant L as Ledger ⏎   A->>R: confirm transfer, B, 8000 cents ⏎   R->>D: save pending record with client ID ⏎   R->>S: POST transfer, client ID, amount ⏎   S->>L: check balance, debit A, credit B in one transaction ⏎   L-->>S: transfer record, status ⏎   S-->>R: transfer record, status ⏎   R->>D: update record status ⏎   R-->>A: result state ⏎   A->>A: show success from server record
card.then: Next I'd cover the failure case: a timeout or lost response, and how the app finds out what really happened.

more: The screen shows success only from the server's transfer record, not from the local pending row. If the response is lost, the app doesn't know yet, so it shows "still checking". It asks the server again with the same client transfer ID. The server must answer a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, not a second payment.

diagram.type: draw@wallet sequence: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as Screen and ViewModel

judge.detail: PASS: The sequenceDiagram covers confirm, submit with client transfer ID, atomic server debit/credit, response, and result; SAY covers amounts in cents (8000) and final balances (A 20, B 80) and result states (success from server record, pending/"still checking").
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirm, submit with a client transfer ID, an atomic server debit and credit, the response and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents and the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and the result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the repository writes a pending record to the local database before sending the request — what exactly goes into that pending row, and how does the app use it if the process is killed before the response comes back?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: what goes into the pending row, and how the app uses it after process death
card.say: The pending row holds the client transfer ID, the payer and recipient, the amount as 8000 cents, and a status of pending. It's written to the local database before the request goes out, so it survives process death. When the app starts again, the repository finds rows still pending and asks the server for each one by its client ID. The screen shows "still checking" until the server's record says success or a clear failure.
card.then: Next I'd cover the result screen states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown.

more: The row also needs a timestamp and a retry count, and I'd back off between retries with the same client ID so repeated restarts don't hammer the server.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies the pending row contents (client transfer ID, payer/recipient, 8000 cents, pending status), explains it's written before the request so it survives process death, and describes startup recovery by querying the server per client ID — all consistent with the earlier sequence diagram and the server's idempotent-by-client-ID behavior, with no invented facts.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence shows "R->>D: update record status" right after the server response, which assumes that response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before that update — when A reopens the app, what changes in your flow? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: server committed, response lost, process killed — update the sequence
card.say: The pending row stays pending, because the update never ran. When A reopens the app, the repository finds that row and asks the server by the same client ID. The server returns the original record, so the screen shows success. The local row is only a note; the server's record is the truth.
card.type: replace@sequenceDiagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as Screen and ViewModel ⏎   participant R as Repository ⏎   participant D as Local DB ⏎   participant S as Server ⏎   A->>R: confirm transfer, B, 8000 cents ⏎   R->>D: save pending record with client ID ⏎   R->>S: POST transfer, client ID, amount ⏎   S-->>R: response lost, process killed ⏎   Note over R,D: row stays pending ⏎   A->>R: app reopened ⏎   R->>D: read pending rows ⏎   R->>S: GET transfer by client ID ⏎   S-->>R: original record, success ⏎   R->>D: update record status ⏎   R-->>A: success from server record
card.then: Next I'd cover the result screen states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown.

more: The restart lookup needs a limit: if the server still has no record after a few tries, I'd keep the state unknown and tell the user to check history later, and I'd never show a failure, because the money may have moved.

diagram.type: replace@sequenceDiagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as Screen and ViewMod

judge.detail: PASS: The answer keeps the pending row with the client transfer ID persisted before sending, queries the server by that same ID after restart, shows the server's original record as truth (success), and the next card explicitly says to keep the state unknown rather than failed when no record is found — covering the required points with nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeat of the same ID; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said if the server still has no record after a few tries you'd keep it unknown and never show failure — but what if that lookup returns not found because the original request never actually reached the server?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: lookup returns not found — what if the request never reached the server?
card.say: That's the real gap. A not-found answer can't tell me "no money moved" from "the request is still on its way". So I'd keep the state unknown and never show failure. The user sees "still checking" and can open history later. If they want, I could add a server-side expiry: after a set time with no record, the server marks that client ID as expired, and then the app can safely show a clear failure.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer acknowledges the gap, explains why not-found is ambiguous, keeps the unknown state consistent with earlier answers, and adds a specific server-side expiry mechanism without inventing any employer, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: two phones, two 80 dollar transfers at the same time
card.say: Each phone sends its own request with its own client ID, so they're two separate transfers. The server handles them one at a time in the ledger. The first one takes A from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80. The second one fails the balance check, because A only has 20 dollars left. So one phone shows success, and the other shows a clear failure: not enough money.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two transfers as separate intents with their own client IDs, has the server process them one at a time in the ledger, shows the first succeeding (A 100→20, B 0→80) and the second failing the balance check for insufficient funds, with one phone showing success and the other a clear failure.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result"]
card.heard: account switch while A's response is in flight
card.say: The old response could land on C's screen. So I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation. When the response comes back, the repository checks the generation. If it's old, it drops the response and never writes it to the local database. The money A already sent stays on the server, and A sees it in history after signing in again.
card.type: draw@sequence diagram for account switch: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as Account A screen ⏎   participant R as Repository ⏎   participant S as Server ⏎   participant C as Account C screen ⏎   A->>R: confirm transfer, session 1 ⏎   R->>S: POST transfer, client ID, session 1 ⏎   C->>R: switch to account C, session 2 ⏎   S-->>R: response for session 1 ⏎   R->>R: session 1 is old, drop it ⏎   R-->>C: no update, C keeps its own state
card.then: Next: what happens to A's pending row after the drop.

more: The old response must not touch C's data. If the generation is old, it drops the response and leaves A's pending row alone. A's row stays pending, and the next lookup for A resolves it.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer tags requests with account and session generation, drops the stale response so C never sees A's data, and notes A's committed transfer appears in A's history after signing in again.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said the local row is only a note and the server's record is the truth — now the pilot starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see when the stream is gone? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result", "Pilot entry from a group chat: the chat only suggests a payment; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, so the app asks the user to pick the recipient and enter the amount", "The chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms; the transfer still goes out and the screen shows the unknown state until the server record answers"]
card.heard: chat says "pay Alex", two Alexes, no amount, stream drops after confirm
card.say: Two things change. The chat only gives me a hint, not a payment. So the app opens a native confirm screen with the recipient and the amount, and the user fills in what's missing. With two contacts named Alex, I'd show both and ask which one, and I'd never guess the amount. The server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry, so chat text never authorizes money.
card.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> B[App: open confirm screen] ⏎   B --> C[User picks Alex and enters amount] ⏎   C --> D[Repository: pending row, client ID] ⏎   D --> E[Server: check and move money] ⏎   E --> F[Transfer record: status] ⏎   F --> G[Screen: success or still checking]
card.then: Next: what the confirm screen shows when the stream is already gone.

more: The confirm screen shows the recipient, the amount and the balance. When the stream is gone, the screen says "still checking" and keeps the pending row. The transfer still goes out, because the confirm already happened on our own screen. If the user closes the app, the restart lookup by the same client ID resolves it.

diagram.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> B[App: op

judge.detail: PASS: The answer asks the user to pick which Alex and enter the amount, shows a native confirm screen with recipient and amount, binds server-side authorization to payer/recipient/amount/expiry, keeps the transfer going after the stream drops with "still checking" and restart lookup by client ID, and never lets chat text authorize money; the TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the entry flow.
judge.criterion: SAY asks the user which Alex and what amount, shows a trusted native confirmation with recipient and amount, binds authorization to those parameters server-side, ties a repeated tool call to the original intent, and recovers status from the payment service when the chat drops; the model never authorizes. TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of that entry flow.

turns.name: W6-dyn
turns.question: You said the server binds authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry — so if the group chat later says "actually send it to the other Alex," what does your confirm screen do with that authorization?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result", "Pilot entry from a group chat: the chat only suggests a payment; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, so the app asks the user to pick the recipient and enter the amount", "The chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms; the transfer still goes out and the screen shows the unknown state until the server record answers"]
card.heard: chat says send to the other Alex after confirm
card.say: The old authorization stays bound to the first Alex, the amount and its expiry. So the new chat message can't change it. The app would open a fresh confirm screen for the other Alex, with a new amount and a new client ID. The first transfer still goes out as confirmed, and the user sees both in history.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer correctly keeps the old authorization bound to the first Alex, amount, and expiry, opens a fresh confirm with a new client ID for the other Alex, and stays consistent with the candidate's earlier "chat never authorizes money" and server-bound authorization points without inventing any new wallet rule or employer detail.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W7-release
turns.question: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result", "Pilot entry from a group chat: the chat only suggests a payment; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, so the app asks the user to pick the recipient and enter the amount", "The chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms; the transfer still goes out and the screen shows the unknown state until the server record answers", "Two weeks, with login and a usable ledger already built"]
card.heard: two weeks, first version, sign-off, spike in pending transfers
card.say: For the first version, I'd ship the person-to-person path only: balance, transfer, history and details. The chat entry waits, because it needs the confirm screen and the expiry rule tested first. The product lead signs off on the user flow, and the tech lead signs off on the ledger and the idempotency contract. If pending transfers spike, I'd first check whether it's the server or the app. I'd pause new transfers, keep reads and status working, and have the backend owner reconcile the pending rows by client ID.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer scopes v1 to balance, transfer, history and details, defers chat entry pending confirm/expiry testing, and on a pending-transfer spike pauses new transfers while keeping reads and status working with backend reconciliation by client ID. It does not list the pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch), but the criterion's "does not" conditions are not violated and the other required elements are covered.
judge.criterion: SAY cuts scope to balance, internal transfer, history, confirmation and recoverable states; lists pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch); on a spike pauses new submissions while keeping reads and status, owners reconcile, then resume.

turns.name: W7-dyn
turns.question: You said you'd pause new transfers and have the backend owner reconcile pending rows by client ID — in that half hour, what would you personally own, who do you need beside you, and at what signal would you escalate to me?

card.constraints: ["MVP path is person-to-person payment: pick a recipient, enter an amount, confirm, and see the result", "Pilot entry from a group chat: the chat only suggests a payment; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, so the app asks the user to pick the recipient and enter the amount", "The chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms; the transfer still goes out and the screen shows the unknown state until the server record answers", "Two weeks, with login and a usable ledger already built"]
card.heard: what I personally own in the half hour, who beside me, escalation signal
card.say: In that half hour I'd own the client side. I'd check whether the spike comes from our app or the server, and I'd keep the status screen honest for users. I need the backend owner beside me to reconcile pending rows by client ID, and QA to check the app path. I'd escalate to you if the pending count keeps rising after we pause, or if any user's balance looks wrong.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names what the candidate personally owns (client side, checking app vs server, keeping status honest), who is beside them (backend owner for reconciliation by client ID, QA), and an escalation signal (pending count still rising after pause, or wrong balances) — all consistent with earlier answers and inventing no new rules or credentials.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: Q-close
turns.question: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?

card.problem: Ask the interviewer questions about the team and the role
card.heard: any questions for me about the team or the role
card.say: Yes, I have two. First, what would make you feel you hired the right Android engineer six months from now? Second, what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, partial results, or reliable actions?

judge.detail: PASS: The candidate asks two sensible founder questions—success criteria six months post-hire and the biggest current mobile challenge—neither of which was answered earlier in the conversation.
judge.criterion: SAY asks one or two sensible questions to a founder that were not already answered in this conversation.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: Good evening, and thank you for the introduction.
Candidate: The project I'd pick is the product page at KKday, because it's the most hands-on Android work I've done.
Candidate: Travelers used it to choose a tour, a date and a ticket type, and the price and stock had to update on every tap.
Candidate: Before my change, each tap took about one second, which felt slow.
Candidate: I rebuilt how the data was prepared, moved the heavy calculation off the main thread, and sent results through StateFlow.

Interviewer: On the KKday product page, you said you rebuilt how the data was prepared and moved the heavy calculation off the main thread — which exact parts of that did you build yourself versus the rest of the team?
Candidate: I built the SKU calculation myself.
Candidate: I flattened the configuration and built the price and stock index.
Candidate: I moved the work to Dispatchers.Default and sent results through StateFlow.
Candidate: The caching and skeleton screens were also my work.
Candidate: The backend product data and the design came from other teams.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: I'll take one tap on a ticket type.
Candidate: The tap goes to the ViewModel, and it updates the selected options in a StateFlow.
Candidate: The calculation runs on Dispatchers.Default, not on the main thread.
Candidate: It looks up the price and stock in the index I built ahead of time, then sends the new result back through StateFlow.
Candidate: The screen collects that state and redraws the price and stock.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a wrong price after a fast double tap.
Candidate: My first guess was the network, so I logged the request and response.
Candidate: The data was correct every time.
Candidate: Then I reproduced it by tapping two options quickly.
Candidate: The second tap read the old index before the first result came back.
Interviewer: You said the second tap read the old index before the first result came back — how did you actually confirm that was the root cause rather than just a plausible story?
Candidate: I confirmed it with a log line.
Candidate: I printed the selected option and the index version each time the calculation ran.
Candidate: In the fast double tap, the second line showed the old version number.
Candidate: When I added the version check, the wrong price stopped.
Candidate: I also ran the same double tap ten times before and after the fix.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had two other options.
Candidate: One was to lock the calculation with a mutex, so only one ran at a time.
Candidate: The other was to cancel the old job when a new tap came in.
Candidate: I didn't pick the mutex because it would still queue the taps and make the page feel slow.
Candidate: I didn't pick cancel-and-restart because a fast double tap would throw away the first result, and the user would see a flicker.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, I found a broken back button in some old pages during testing, just before a release.
Candidate: I told the project manager that same day.
Candidate: I gave two options: ship everything else and move my change to the next release, or ship it all and accept the risk.
Candidate: He decided to move my change.
Candidate: I kept checking the other pages and fixed the back button myself.

Interviewer: You said the PM chose to move your change and you fixed the back button yourself — before that release, what risk were you personally willing to accept, who watched the data afterward, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: I was willing to accept the risk on the pages I hadn't checked yet, because the back button only affected navigation, not prices or orders.
Candidate: I told the PM that clearly, so he decided with the real picture.
Candidate: For the release, I ran the checks we already had: the fast double tap ten times, the price and stock on each option, and the back button on every page I could reach.
Candidate: Everything else shipped on time.
Candidate: After release, I watched the crash rate in Bugly and the reports from QA and support.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design anything, I'd like to check a few things.
Candidate: Who are the users: friends sending money to each other, or a business paying people?
Candidate: Where does the money balance really live: only on our server, or also with a bank or card partner?
Candidate: And what should work offline: can someone start a transfer with no network, or should the app just show the last known balance?
Candidate: Does that match what you want?

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, the rules are clear.
Candidate: The screen shows the balance and the transfer form, and it only reads state from the ViewModel.
Candidate: The ViewModel calls the repository, and the repository is the only place that talks to the network and the local database.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Screen: balance, transfer form] --> B[ViewModel: state] |   B --> C[Repository] |   C --> D[Local DB: cached balance and history] |   C --> E[Server API] |   E --> F[Ledger: accounts, transfers]
Candidate: The board already shows the three parts.
Candidate: The screen and ViewModel own only what the user sees.
Candidate: The repository owns the data rules, and the local database is a cache for offline reads.
Candidate: The server owns the ledger, so it decides every balance and limit.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars.
Candidate: A confirms on the screen, and the ViewModel sends the transfer to the repository.
Candidate: The repository writes a pending record to the local database and sends the request with a client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server checks A's balance, then debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Candidate: A goes from 100 to 20 dollars, and B goes from 0 to 80.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as Screen and ViewModel |   participant R as Repository |   participant D as Local DB |   participant S as Server |   participant L as Ledger |   A->>R: confirm transfer, B, 8000 cents |   R->>D: save pending record with client ID |   R->>S: POST transfer, client ID, amount |   S->>L: check balance, debit A, credit B in one transaction |   L-->>S: transfer record, status |   S-->>R: transfer record, status |   R->>D: update record status |   R-->>A: result state |   A->>A: show success from server record
Candidate: The screen shows success only from the server's transfer record, not from the local pending row.
Candidate: If the response is lost, the app doesn't know yet, so it shows "still checking".
Candidate: It asks the server again with the same client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server must answer a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, not a second payment.

Interviewer: You said the repository writes a pending record to the local database before sending the request — what exactly goes into that pending row, and how does the app use it if the process is killed before the response comes back?
Candidate: The pending row holds the client transfer ID, the payer and recipient, the amount as 8000 cents, and a status of pending.
Candidate: It's written to the local database before the request goes out, so it survives process death.
Candidate: When the app starts again, the repository finds rows still pending and asks the server for each one by its client ID.
Candidate: The screen shows "still checking" until the server's record says success or a clear failure.
Candidate: The row also needs a timestamp and a retry count, and I'd back off between retries with the same client ID so repeated restarts don't hammer the server.

Interviewer: Your sequence shows "R->>D: update record status" right after the server response, which assumes that response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before that update — when A reopens the app, what changes in your flow? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: The pending row stays pending, because the update never ran.
Candidate: When A reopens the app, the repository finds that row and asks the server by the same client ID.
Candidate: The server returns the original record, so the screen shows success.
Candidate: The local row is only a note; the server's record is the truth.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as Screen and ViewModel |   participant R as Repository |   participant D as Local DB |   participant S as Server |   A->>R: confirm transfer, B, 8000 cents |   R->>D: save pending record with client ID |   R->>S: POST transfer, client ID, amount |   S-->>R: response lost, process killed |   Note over R,D: row stays pending |   A->>R: app reopened |   R->>D: read pending rows |   R->>S: GET transfer by client ID |   S-->>R: original record, success |   R->>D: update record status |   R-->>A: success from server record

Candidate: The restart lookup needs a limit: if the server still has no record after a few tries, I'd keep the state unknown and tell the user to check history later, and I'd never show a failure, because the money may have moved.

Interviewer: You said if the server still has no record after a few tries you'd keep it unknown and never show failure — but what if that lookup returns not found because the original request never actually reached the server?
Candidate: That's the real gap.
Candidate: A not-found answer can't tell me "no money moved" from "the request is still on its way".
Candidate: So I'd keep the state unknown and never show failure.
Candidate: The user sees "still checking" and can open history later.
Candidate: If they want, I could add a server-side expiry: after a set time with no record, the server marks that client ID as expired, and then the app can safely show a clear failure.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Each phone sends its own request with its own client ID, so they're two separate transfers.
Candidate: The server handles them one at a time in the ledger.
Candidate: The first one takes A from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, because A only has 20 dollars left.
Candidate: So one phone shows success, and the other shows a clear failure: not enough money.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The old response could land on C's screen.
Candidate: So I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When the response comes back, the repository checks the generation.
Candidate: If it's old, it drops the response and never writes it to the local database.
Candidate: The money A already sent stays on the server, and A sees it in history after signing in again.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as Account A screen |   participant R as Repository |   participant S as Server |   participant C as Account C screen |   A->>R: confirm transfer, session 1 |   R->>S: POST transfer, client ID, session 1 |   C->>R: switch to account C, session 2 |   S-->>R: response for session 1 |   R->>R: session 1 is old, drop it |   R-->>C: no update, C keeps its own state
Candidate: The old response must not touch C's data.
Candidate: If the generation is old, it drops the response and leaves A's pending row alone.
Candidate: A's row stays pending, and the next lookup for A resolves it.

Interviewer: You said the local row is only a note and the server's record is the truth — now the pilot starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see when the stream is gone? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: Two things change.
Candidate: The chat only gives me a hint, not a payment.
Candidate: So the app opens a native confirm screen with the recipient and the amount, and the user fills in what's missing.
Candidate: With two contacts named Alex, I'd show both and ask which one, and I'd never guess the amount.
Candidate: The server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry, so chat text never authorizes money.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> B[App: open confirm screen] |   B --> C[User picks Alex and enters amount] |   C --> D[Repository: pending row, client ID] |   D --> E[Server: check and move money] |   E --> F[Transfer record: status] |   F --> G[Screen: success or still checking]
Candidate: The confirm screen shows the recipient, the amount and the balance.
Candidate: When the stream is gone, the screen says "still checking" and keeps the pending row.
Candidate: The transfer still goes out, because the confirm already happened on our own screen.
Candidate: If the user closes the app, the restart lookup by the same client ID resolves it.

Interviewer: You said the server binds authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry — so if the group chat later says "actually send it to the other Alex," what does your confirm screen do with that authorization?
Candidate: The old authorization stays bound to the first Alex, the amount and its expiry.
Candidate: So the new chat message can't change it.
Candidate: The app would open a fresh confirm screen for the other Alex, with a new amount and a new client ID.
Candidate: The first transfer still goes out as confirmed, and the user sees both in history.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: For the first version, I'd ship the person-to-person path only: balance, transfer, history and details.
Candidate: The chat entry waits, because it needs the confirm screen and the expiry rule tested first.
Candidate: The product lead signs off on the user flow, and the tech lead signs off on the ledger and the idempotency contract.
Candidate: If pending transfers spike, I'd first check whether it's the server or the app.
Candidate: I'd pause new transfers, keep reads and status working, and have the backend owner reconcile the pending rows by client ID.

Interviewer: You said you'd pause new transfers and have the backend owner reconcile pending rows by client ID — in that half hour, what would you personally own, who do you need beside you, and at what signal would you escalate to me?
Candidate: In that half hour I'd own the client side.
Candidate: I'd check whether the spike comes from our app or the server, and I'd keep the status screen honest for users.
Candidate: I need the backend owner beside me to reconcile pending rows by client ID, and QA to check the app path.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you if the pending count keeps rising after we pause, or if any user's balance looks wrong.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: Yes, I have two.
Candidate: First, what would make you feel you hired the right Android engineer six months from now?
Candidate: Second, what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, partial results, or reliable actions?
